name: D1.1 Ethics and the three pillars (CIA)

paragraphes: Your neighbor goes on vacation. He gives you his house keys, so you can water his plants.
You could walk in and look around. Nobody would see you. But you do not do it.
You stay honest, even when nobody watches. A security worker also holds many keys. Their honesty is written in a code of ethics. This is a list of rules that they promise to follow.

decouverte.titre: It is like the rules of a school
decouverte.comme: At school, you agree to the school rules: be honest, respect others, help your classmates. The rules cannot cover every case. You must think too.
decouverte.enVrai: The (ISC)2 code of ethics works the same way. (ISC)2 is the group that gives the CISSP certificate. Its code has four main rules, called canons. They guide your thinking. They do not replace it. A member who breaks the code on purpose can lose the certificate.

decouverte.question: You are an (ISC)2 member. You see another member break the code of ethics. What should you do?
options: Do nothing, because it is not your business
Follow the official complaint steps
Talk to the member in secret and say nothing more
decouverte.explanation: (ISC)2 asks you to follow the official complaint steps. Staying silent can also break the code. The other two choices look kind, but they do not protect the profession.

decouverte.texte: A colleague asks you to read the messages of a person he dislikes. You have the access to do it. But the code asks you to act honestly and to protect public trust. Being able to do something does not mean you have the right to do it.

decouverte.titre: It is like choosing a plumber
decouverte.comme: A plumber comes into your home and sees your things. You pick one with a good name. If you have a doubt about him, you call someone else.
decouverte.enVrai: The preamble is the opening text of the code. It says the same. A member must follow the code and must also be seen following it. Even a doubt can hurt their place. The people you work for are called principals.

cards.question: Official definition: “(ISC)2 Code of Ethics Preamble”
cards.answer: The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.
cards.explanation: In simple words: you must act well, and others must see that you act well. If you break the code, you can lose your certificate.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “(ISC)2 Code of Ethics Preamble”?
options: The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of employment.

The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and be seen to adhere, to the highest legal standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.

The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, but not always be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.

The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.
options_why: The last word changes the idea. The code is a condition of certification, not of employment.
It says legal standards. The real sentence says ethical standards.
It drops the idea of being seen. The real sentence says to adhere, and be seen to adhere.
cards.answer: The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.
cards.explanation: Look at three key parts: be seen to adhere, ethical standards, and a condition of certification.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “(ISC)2 Code of Ethics Preamble” from memory.
cards.answer: The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the good of society, being seen to follow the code, and the condition of certification.

cards.question: Official definition: the role of the four canons
cards.answer: The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics includes four canons that are intended to serve as high-level guidelines to augment, not replace, members' professional judgment.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the four canons are broad rules that help you think. They do not think for you.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official statement about the role of the four canons?
options: The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics includes six canons that are intended to serve as high-level guidelines to augment, not replace, members' professional judgment.
The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics includes four canons that are intended to serve as high-level guidelines to augment, not replace, members' professional judgment.
The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics includes four canons that are intended to serve as high-level guidelines to replace, not augment, members' professional judgment.
The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics includes four canons that are intended to serve as detailed procedures to augment, not replace, members' professional judgment.
options_why: The code has four canons, not six.
The order is reversed. The canons help your judgment. They do not take its place.
The canons are broad guidelines, not detailed procedures.
cards.answer: The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics includes four canons that are intended to serve as high-level guidelines to augment, not replace, members' professional judgment.
cards.explanation: Look at three key parts: four canons, high-level guidelines, and augment, not replace.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about the role of the four canons from memory.
cards.answer: The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics includes four canons that are intended to serve as high-level guidelines to augment, not replace, members' professional judgment.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the number of canons, their role as guides, and the fact that they add to your judgment.

cards.question: Official definition: “Canon I”
cards.answer: Canon I: Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure.
cards.explanation: In simple words: protect people and the services that everyone needs. The infrastructure means things like networks and power.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”. The four canons in order: society, honesty, service to principals, the profession.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “Canon I” from memory.
cards.answer: Canon I: Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure.
cards.explanation: Three parts: protect society, keep public trust, and protect the infrastructure.

cards.question: Official definition: “Canon II”
cards.answer: Canon II: Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally.
cards.explanation: In simple words: be honest and follow the law. The list has five words.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “Canon II” from memory.
cards.answer: Canon II: Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally.
cards.explanation: Five words: honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally.

cards.question: Official definition: “Canon III”
cards.answer: Canon III: Provide diligent and competent service to principals.
cards.explanation: In simple words: do careful and skilled work for the people you work for.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “Canon III” from memory.
cards.answer: Canon III: Provide diligent and competent service to principals.
cards.explanation: Two words describe the work: diligent and competent. It is for principals.

cards.question: Official definition: “Canon IV”
cards.answer: Canon IV: Advance and protect the profession.
cards.explanation: In simple words: help the profession grow and keep its good name.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “Canon IV” from memory.
cards.answer: Canon IV: Advance and protect the profession.
cards.explanation: Two verbs and one noun: advance, protect, the profession.

cards.question: What is the main job of the (ISC)2 code of ethics?
options: To guide the judgment of members
To replace the judgment of members
To give a full step list for every situation
To describe how to test a security tool
options_why: The manual says the canons augment judgment. They do not replace it.
No list can cover every case. The canons are broad guides.
The code is about behavior, not about technical tests.
cards.answer: To guide the judgment of members
cards.explanation: The canons are high-level guides. They help members think. They do not think for them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: An employee tells her client about her own mistake, even though it is hard. Which canon does this match BEST?
options: Canon I: protect society and the infrastructure
Canon II: act honestly and legally
Canon III: give careful service to principals
Canon IV: advance and protect the profession
options_why: This canon is about protecting the public and basic services.
Good service matters, but the key idea here is telling the truth.
This canon is about the good name of the profession.
cards.answer: Canon II: act honestly and legally
cards.explanation: Admitting a mistake is honest behavior. This is the idea of Canon II.

cards.question: What does the preamble say about following the code?
options: Members must follow it only during working hours
Members must follow it only when someone checks
Members must follow it and also be seen following it
Members only need to know it for the exam
options_why: The manual says members must be visible ethical leaders at all times.
The code applies all the time, not only when people look.
Strict adherence is a condition of certification, so it applies in real life.
cards.answer: Members must follow it and also be seen following it
cards.explanation: Members must act well, and others must see it. This is the idea of the preamble.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: You see another (ISC)2 member break the code of ethics. What is the BEST action?
options: Follow the published ethics complaint procedure
Ignore it, because it is a private matter between members
Warn the member in private and keep it secret
Post about it online to warn the other members
options_why: Not acting can be seen as a breach of Canon IV.
This looks kind, but it is not the official procedure.
This looks bold, but it is not the official procedure, and it can hurt the profession.
cards.answer: Follow the published ethics complaint procedure
cards.explanation: (ISC)2 asks members to follow the published complaint procedure. Not doing so may break Canon IV.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: A CISSP jokes online that she breaks into school accounts. She never did it. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: There is no problem, because she did not break any real rule
Only real actions count, and the image she gives is not important
Even the look of bad behavior can hurt her standing
The code bans every joke that a member writes online
options_why: The preamble says that the perception of bad behavior matters too.
Members must be visible ethical leaders, so the image counts.
The code says nothing about jokes. It talks about honest behavior and trust.
cards.answer: Even the look of bad behavior can hurt her standing
cards.explanation: The manual says that even the perception of bad behavior can put a member's standing in question.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four canons of the (ISC)2 code?
options: Protect society, the common good, and public trust
Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally
Provide diligent and competent service to principals
Put the profit of the employer before everything else
options_why: This is the core of Canon I.
This is Canon II.
This is Canon III.
cards.answer: Put the profit of the employer before everything else
cards.explanation: The canons are about society, honesty, service to principals, and the profession. Profit first is not in them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: A manager asks a CISSP to read a colleague's private messages. The CISSP has the access. What is the BEST response?
options: Do it, because the company gave him the access to the system
Refuse, because the code asks for honest and legal behavior
Do it once, but tell nobody about it afterwards, to be safe
Refuse, but give the manager the password to do it
options_why: Having access does not give the right to use it.
Hiding the act is not honest, and the act is still not allowed.
This still helps to read private messages without the right.
cards.answer: Refuse, because the code asks for honest and legal behavior
cards.explanation: The code asks for honest and legal behavior and for public trust. Having the access is not a reason.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this example is ours. It applies the idea of Canon II.

cards.question: Besides the (ISC)2 code, which other code must a security professional know?
options: None, because the (ISC)2 code is enough
Only the laws of the country, but no other codes
The code of ethics of a competitor company
The code of the employer or the industry
options_why: The manual says you must also know the code of your employer or industry.
Laws matter, but the manual also asks for the employer or industry code.
You must follow the rules of your own employer or industry.
cards.answer: The code of the employer or the industry
cards.explanation: Other codes do not replace sound judgment and moral behavior. As a CISSP, you lead by example.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Organizational Code of Ethics”.

cards.question: Which statement BEST describes what can happen to a member who knowingly breaks the code?
options: Peer review, and possibly the loss of the certification
A fine that is paid to the other members of the group
Nothing at all, because the code is only advice for members
A ban from all work in security for the rest of their life
options_why: The manual talks about peer review and penalties such as losing the certification.
The code has real results. A member can face a review.
This is too extreme. The manual does not say this.
cards.answer: Peer review, and possibly the loss of the certification
cards.explanation: A member who knowingly breaks the code faces peer review and possible penalties.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand, Adhere to, and Promote Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: How can a CISSP BEST lead by example inside an organization?
options: By asking others to follow it, but not the managers
By following only the (ISC)2 code and ignoring the employer's code
By following the organization's code of ethics in daily work
By knowing the code but leaving it to the human resources team to follow
options_why: A leader must follow the rules too. Leaders cannot be an exception.
The manual says to follow both codes.
Nobody else can follow the code for you.
cards.answer: By following the organization's code of ethics in daily work
cards.explanation: As a CISSP, you are a leader. You should lead by example in following your organization's code.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Organizational Code of Ethics”.

cards.question: Which action fits Canon IV BEST?
options: Protecting the network of a whole city from an attack
Using the complaint steps when a member breaks the code
Telling a client the truth about a mistake that she made
Giving a client careful and skilled work every day
options_why: This is Canon I: protecting society and the infrastructure.
This is Canon II: honest behavior.
This is Canon III: service to principals.
cards.answer: Using the complaint steps when a member breaks the code
cards.explanation: Canon IV is about the profession. Not following the complaint steps may be a breach of Canon IV.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: What does “principals” mean in the code of ethics?
cards.answer: The people you work for, such as your employer and your clients.
cards.explanation: Canon III is about serving principals with care.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: the manual does not explain this word. This is its usual meaning here.

cards.question: What can happen to a member who knowingly breaks the code?
cards.answer: Peer review and possible penalties. These can include losing the certification.
cards.explanation: The code is not only advice. It has real results.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand, Adhere to, and Promote Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: Why does the code not replace your own judgment?
cards.answer: The canons are broad guides. No list can cover every case, so you must think too.
cards.explanation: The canons help you think. They do not think for you.

cards.question: What does “be seen to adhere” mean?
cards.answer: You must follow the code, and others must see that you follow it. Even the look of bad behavior can hurt your standing.
cards.explanation: Think of the plumber: you want one with a good name.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

concepts.name: Information security and the CIA Triad

paragraphes: Your school keeps all your grades in a big register. These grades are information, and they have value.
Think of all that could go wrong with this register. Protecting information is the job of information security.
Experts sum up this job in three pillars. They call them the CIA Triad.

decouverte.comme: Your diary has a lock. Problem one: a curious person reads it. Problem two: someone scribbles on your pages. Problem three: you lose the key and cannot open it.
decouverte.enVrai: The curious reader is a loss of confidentiality. The scribbles are a loss of integrity. The lost key is a loss of availability. Keep this diary in mind. We will use it in the next planets.

decouverte.question: In an online shop, one hacker copies the customer addresses. A second hacker changes all prices to one euro. A third hacker shuts the site on sale day. How many pillars are hit?
options: Only one
Two
All three, one for each attack
decouverte.answer: All three, one for each attack
decouverte.explanation: Copying addresses breaks secrecy. Changing prices breaks accuracy. Shutting the site breaks access. Each attack hits a different pillar.

decouverte.comme: A tripod stands on three legs. If one leg is missing, the camera falls.
decouverte.enVrai: The CIA Triad has three pillars that work together. The letters stand for three English words. They have nothing to do with the spy agency of the same name. The image stops here: a tripod has no favorite leg, but a company can care more about one pillar.

decouverte.texte: A hospital keeps a file for each patient. Only the care team should read it. A dose of medicine must never change by mistake. And the file must open fast in the emergency room. Three needs, three pillars.

cards.question: Official definition: “information security”
cards.answer: Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in safeguarding information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disturbance.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the methods that protect information and its systems from bad access, use, change, or disruption.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand and Apply Security Concepts”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “information security”?
options: Information security refers to the tools and products involved in safeguarding information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disturbance.
Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in safeguarding only information from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disturbance.
Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in safeguarding information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disturbance.
Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in safeguarding information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disclosure.
options_why: The real sentence says processes and methodologies, not tools and products.
The real sentence also covers the underlying systems.
The last danger is disturbance, not disclosure.
cards.answer: Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in safeguarding information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disturbance.
cards.explanation: Look at the key parts: processes and methodologies, underlying systems, and the four dangers.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “information security” from memory.
cards.answer: Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in safeguarding information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disturbance.
cards.explanation: Four dangers to remember: access, use, modification, and disturbance.

cards.question: Official definition: “CIA Triad”
cards.answer: This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the pillars of information security known as the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation: In simple words: confidentiality, integrity, and availability are the three pillars of information security. Together they are the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand and Apply Security Concepts”. The word “This” at the start means information security.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “CIA Triad”?
options: This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity. Together, these three principles form the pillars of information security known as the CIA Triad.

This is most often described by five critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the pillars of information security known as the CIA Triad.

This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the tools of information security known as the CIA Triad.

This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the pillars of information security known as the CIA Triad.
options_why: The third concept is availability, not authenticity.
The triad has three concepts, not five.
They are the pillars of information security, not tools.
cards.answer: This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the pillars of information security known as the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation: Look at the three words, the number three, and the word pillars.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “CIA Triad” from memory.
cards.answer: This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the pillars of information security known as the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation: Three parts: three concepts, the pillars of information security, and the name CIA Triad.

cards.question: In the name CIA Triad, what does the letter A stand for?
options: Availability
Authenticity
Accountability
Accessibility
options_why: This is a related idea, but it is not the A of the triad.
This idea is not part of the triad.
This word is close to availability, but it is not the A of the triad.
cards.answer: Availability
cards.explanation: The A is for availability: authorized people can reach the data when they need it.

cards.question: A hacker changes the price of an item to one euro on a website. Which pillar is hit?
options: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
None, because the site still works
options_why: Nobody read secret data. A price was changed.
The site still works. A price was changed.
The data became incorrect, so a pillar is hit.
cards.answer: Integrity
cards.explanation: Nothing was read in secret. Some data was changed, and changing data is a loss of integrity.

cards.question: Doctors cannot open the patient files in the emergency room. Nobody read or changed the files. Which pillar is hit?
options: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authenticity
options_why: Nobody read the files without the right.
The files were not changed. They are just out of reach.
This is not a pillar of the triad.
cards.answer: Availability
cards.explanation: Authorized people cannot reach the data when they need it. This is a loss of availability.

cards.question: A new employee asks what the CIA Triad is. Which answer is BEST?
options: Three tools that a company must buy and install
Three jobs that people have in the security team
Three steps that a company does in a fixed order
Three goals that work together to protect data
options_why: A tool is something you buy. The triad is a set of goals.
The three words are ideas, not job titles.
The three work together. They are not steps in an order.
cards.answer: Three goals that work together to protect data
cards.explanation: The triad has three goals: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. They work together.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand and Apply Security Concepts”.

cards.question: Which statement about the three pillars is MOST accurate?
options: They work together, and some systems favor one
They are separate, so a company needs only one
Confidentiality always matters more than the other two pillars
They are used one after another, in a fixed order
options_why: The manual says that all three depend on each other.
Different systems can put the focus on a different pillar.
They work together at the same time, not in an order.
cards.answer: They work together, and some systems favor one
cards.explanation: Different systems may favor one pillar, but all three work together and depend on each other.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand and Apply Security Concepts”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a pillar of the CIA Triad?
options: Confidentiality
Authenticity
Integrity
Availability
options_why: This is the first pillar.
This is the second pillar.
This is the third pillar.
cards.answer: Authenticity
cards.explanation: The three pillars are confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Authenticity is a related idea, but not a pillar.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand and Apply Security Concepts”.

cards.question: A storm floods the server room. The data is not read or changed, but the shop cannot sell. Which pillar is hit?
options: Availability
Confidentiality
Integrity
All three, because a flood damages everything
options_why: Nobody saw data they should not see.
The data was not changed.
The data was not read or changed, so only one pillar is hit.
cards.answer: Availability
cards.explanation: People cannot reach the systems and data. A flood or a power cut hurts availability, even with no hacker.

cards.question: Which situation is a loss of integrity?
options: A visitor reads a sales report over a worker's shoulder
A virus changes the numbers in a sales report
A power cut turns off the report server
A student forgets the password of the report folder
options_why: This is a loss of confidentiality.
This is a loss of availability.
This is a loss of availability, because the report cannot be reached.
cards.answer: A virus changes the numbers in a sales report
cards.explanation: Data was changed without the right to do so. This is a loss of integrity.

cards.question: How is information security different from the CIA Triad?
options: They are the same thing, only with two different names
The triad is a software tool that replaces most security work
Security is the whole job, and the triad names its pillars
Information security is only one pillar of the triad
options_why: Information security is the protection work. The triad is its three pillars.
The triad is a way to describe the goals. It does not replace anything.
It is the other way round. The triad forms the pillars of information security.
cards.answer: Security is the whole job, and the triad names its pillars
cards.explanation: Information security is the work of protecting information. The three pillars of the triad describe its goals.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand and Apply Security Concepts”.

cards.question: A company keeps public brochures and secret designs. The manager wants to use the CIA Triad. What should she do FIRST?
options: Buy the strongest tool for each pillar
Give every kind of data the same protection, to keep it simple
Remove all access to the secret designs
Decide which pillar matters most for each data type
options_why: Tools come after the needs are clear.
Different data needs different protection.
This is extreme. People still need the data to work.
cards.answer: Decide which pillar matters most for each data type
cards.explanation: Different types of data may favor different pillars. Understand the need first, then choose the tools.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand and Apply Security Concepts”.

cards.question: Why do security professionals share one meaning for each pillar?
options: So that every company has to buy the same security tools
So that the exam questions can be shorter and easier
So that they can talk about security in a clear way
So that every company has the same risks and threats
options_why: The shared meaning helps people talk. It does not choose tools.
The goal is clear communication in real work.
Each company has its own risks. The shared meaning only helps communication.
cards.answer: So that they can talk about security in a clear way
cards.explanation: A common understanding of each pillar lets professionals communicate well.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand and Apply Security Concepts”.

cards.question: Explain the CIA Triad to a friend in your own words.
cards.answer: Three goals that protect information. Confidentiality: only the right people can see it. Integrity: nobody changes it without the right. Availability: the right people can use it when they need it.
cards.explanation: Think of the diary: the lock, the ink, and the key.

cards.question: Why do we say the three pillars depend on each other?
cards.answer: One pillar alone is not enough. Data that is secret but incorrect, or correct but impossible to open, is useless.
cards.explanation: The three work together to protect information.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand and Apply Security Concepts”.

cards.question: Do the letters CIA in the triad have a link with the spy agency?
cards.answer: No. They only stand for confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
cards.explanation: Same letters, but a different thing.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this is a common source of confusion.

cards.question: What does information security protect, and from what?
cards.answer: It protects information and its systems from improper access, use, change, or disruption.
cards.explanation: This is the short version of the official definition.

paragraphes: You write your secrets in a diary. You put a lock on it.
One day, someone opens it in secret, reads it, and closes it again. Nothing is changed. The pages are all there.
But something is lost: your secrets are not secret now. In security, this is called losing confidentiality.

decouverte.titre: It is like the lock on the diary
decouverte.comme: The lock does not stop the diary from existing. It decides who can read it.
decouverte.enVrai: Confidentiality means that only the right people can see the information. Everyone else is kept out. For a company, the diary is its data: customer files, passwords, secret plans.

decouverte.question: A thief takes a photo of your diary and moves nothing. What is broken?
options: The text is not correct any more
You cannot open your diary any more
The secret: someone read it
decouverte.explanation: The text is the same and you can still open the diary. But someone saw what they should not see. The other two answers are tempting. They are two other goals of security, and you will meet them in the next planets.

decouverte.titre: An email to the wrong person
decouverte.texte: A worker wants to send the salary list to the HR team. She clicks the wrong name, and everyone in the company gets the list. There is no hacker and no broken file. But confidentiality is lost. One simple mistake is enough.

decouverte.comme: In a school, the guard has the key to the teachers room, but not the key to the head teacher's office. Each person has only the keys that they need.
decouverte.enVrai: This is least privilege: each person gets only the access that their job needs. Fewer keys means fewer chances of a leak.

cards.question: Official definition: “confidentiality”
cards.answer: Confidentiality is the concept of limiting access to data to authorized users and systems and restricting access from unauthorized parties.
cards.explanation: In simple words: only the right people and systems can see the data. Everyone else is kept out.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Confidentiality”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “confidentiality”?
options: Confidentiality is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.
Confidentiality is the concept of ensuring that authorized users can access data when they need it.
Confidentiality is the concept of limiting access to data to authorized users and systems and restricting access from unauthorized parties.
Confidentiality is the concept of limiting access to data to administrators and restricting access from all other systems.
options_why: This sentence is about integrity: keeping data correct and complete.
This sentence is about availability: reaching data when you need it.
It looks close, but the real sentence says authorized users and systems, not only administrators.
cards.answer: Confidentiality is the concept of limiting access to data to authorized users and systems and restricting access from unauthorized parties.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: limiting access, authorized users and systems, unauthorized parties.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “confidentiality” from memory.
cards.answer: Confidentiality is the concept of limiting access to data to authorized users and systems and restricting access from unauthorized parties.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: limit access, for authorized users and systems, and keep everyone else out.

cards.question: Official definition: “least privilege”
cards.answer: Under least privilege, users are only given enough access to do their jobs — no more and no less.
cards.explanation: In simple words: give each person the access that the job needs. Not too much, not too little.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Confidentiality”. The manual links it to need-to-know: access to information is given only when a person needs to know it.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “least privilege”?
options: Under least privilege, users are given full access first, and extra access is removed later.
Under least privilege, users are only given enough access to do their jobs — no more and no less.
Under least privilege, users are only given enough access to do their jobs — and a little more, for safety.
Under least privilege, managers are given access to everything that their team can see.
options_why: It starts with full access. Least privilege starts with only what the job needs.
A little more, for safety, is still too much. The words are no more and no less.
Managers do not get extra access just because they are managers. Access follows the job.
cards.answer: Under least privilege, users are only given enough access to do their jobs — no more and no less.
cards.explanation: The key words are: only, enough, to do their jobs, no more and no less.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about “least privilege” from memory.
cards.answer: Under least privilege, users are only given enough access to do their jobs — no more and no less.
cards.explanation: Remember three parts: only, enough access, no more and no less.

cards.question: Official definition: “PII”
cards.answer: Information that can be used to uniquely identify a person, such as names, birthdates, and Social Security numbers, are considered personally identifiable information (PII), which is usually required by law to be kept highly confidential.
cards.explanation: In simple words: PII is any data that points to one exact person. The law usually says it must stay very private.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Confidentiality”. PII stands for personally identifiable information.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about “PII” from memory.
cards.answer: Information that can be used to uniquely identify a person, such as names, birthdates, and Social Security numbers, are considered personally identifiable information (PII), which is usually required by law to be kept highly confidential.
cards.explanation: Three parts: it identifies one person, its name is PII, and the law says it must be kept highly confidential.

cards.question: A worker sends the salary list to the wrong person by mistake. Which security goal is lost?
options: Confidentiality
Availability
Integrity
None, because nobody attacked the company
options_why: Nobody lost access to the list. The people who need it can still reach it.
Nobody changed the list. It is still correct.
Confidentiality can be lost by a simple mistake. An attacker is not needed.
cards.answer: Confidentiality
cards.explanation: Someone who should not see the list can now see it. This is exactly what confidentiality must stop.

cards.question: Which situation is a problem for confidentiality?
options: A server is turned off during a power cut
A visitor reads a private screen over a worker's shoulder
A typing mistake changes a price in a database
A hard disk breaks and files are lost
options_why: People cannot reach the server. That is a problem of availability.
A price became wrong. That is a problem of integrity.
The files cannot be reached any more. That is a problem of availability.
cards.answer: A visitor reads a private screen over a worker's shoulder
cards.explanation: A person who should not see the data can see it. That is a loss of confidentiality.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Confidentiality”: showing sensitive information on a screen near unauthorized viewers is one of the examples.

cards.question: What is the main goal of confidentiality?
options: Keep the data correct
Keep the systems running all day
Keep a record of who did what
Keep the data away from people who should not see it
options_why: That is the goal of integrity.
That is the goal of availability.
That is about tracing actions. It is a different idea.
cards.answer: Keep the data away from people who should not see it
cards.explanation: Confidentiality is about who can see the data.

cards.question: A new employee joins the accounting team. The manager wants her to start work quickly. What is the BEST way to set up her access?
options: Copy the access of the most senior accountant
Give her full access now and remove what she does not use after a month
Give her only the access that an accountant needs for the job
Give her access to all company files so she never needs to ask
options_why: A senior person often has more access than the job needs. Copying it gives her too much.
Starting with full access is risky. A leak can happen in the first month.
This is the fastest way to start, but it gives far too much access and breaks least privilege.
cards.answer: Give her only the access that an accountant needs for the job
cards.explanation: Least privilege: start with what the job needs, and add more only when there is a good reason.

cards.question: Which of these is the BEST example of a control that protects confidentiality?
options: A sign-in step that needs a password and a code from a phone
A daily backup of all the files
A second server that starts when the first one fails
A tool that checks if files were changed
options_why: A backup helps to get data back. That is about availability, not about who can see the data.
A second server keeps the service running. That is about availability.
Checking for changes protects integrity, not confidentiality.
cards.answer: A sign-in step that needs a password and a code from a phone
cards.explanation: A second check at sign-in keeps unauthorized people out. That protects confidentiality.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a good way to protect confidentiality?
options: Training staff to check the email address before they send
Encrypting private files
Using roles to decide who can see what
Giving every worker access to every file
options_why: Training is a good way. Many leaks come from human mistakes.
Encryption is a good way. Without the key, the file cannot be read.
Access by role is a good way. People see only what their role needs.
cards.answer: Giving every worker access to every file
cards.explanation: More people with access means more chances of a leak. This is the opposite of least privilege.

cards.question: Which employee MOST needs access to the salary files?
options: A sales manager who wants to compare her pay
A payroll clerk who prepares the monthly salaries
The receptionist who answers the phone
A new intern who is curious about the company
options_why: Wanting to compare is not a job need. Curiosity is not a good reason.
Answering the phone does not need salary data.
Being curious is not a job need.
cards.answer: A payroll clerk who prepares the monthly salaries
cards.explanation: Access follows the job. The payroll clerk needs the files to do the work.

cards.question: Which of these data is usually PII?
options: The price of a product
The name of a software tool
A date of birth
The color of a company logo
options_why: A price does not point to one person.
A tool name does not point to one person.
A color does not point to one person.
cards.answer: A date of birth
cards.explanation: PII is data that can point to one exact person, like a name or a date of birth.

cards.question: Apart from attackers, what can also cause a loss of confidentiality?
options: Only broken hardware
Only natural disasters
Nothing, because only attackers can do it
Human mistakes, such as sending an email to the wrong person
options_why: Broken hardware mostly hurts availability.
Floods and fires mostly hurt availability.
The manual says that human error, oversight, and negligence can also break confidentiality.
cards.answer: Human mistakes, such as sending an email to the wrong person
cards.explanation: Mistakes are a common cause of leaks. This is why staff training is an important control.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Confidentiality”.

cards.question: How are privacy and confidentiality related?
options: Privacy is about the confidentiality of personal data
They are the same word, so there is no difference
Privacy is about keeping systems available
Privacy is only about passwords
options_why: Privacy is a narrower idea. It is about personal data only, while confidentiality covers all sensitive data.
Keeping systems available is availability, not privacy.
Passwords can help, but privacy is about personal data in general.
cards.answer: Privacy is about the confidentiality of personal data
cards.explanation: Privacy is the part of confidentiality that protects data about people.

cards.question: What is the goal of confidentiality? Say it in your own words.
cards.answer: Only the right people can see the information. Everyone else is kept out.
cards.explanation: Think of the lock on the diary.

cards.question: Name three controls that help to protect confidentiality.
cards.answer: Encryption, multi-factor sign-in (a second check besides the password), and access based on a person's role. Staff training also helps.
cards.explanation: The first three keep unauthorized people out. Training cuts human mistakes.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Confidentiality”: encryption, multifactor authentication, and role-based access controls, plus training.

cards.question: What does PII stand for, and what is it?
cards.answer: Personally identifiable information. It is data that can point to one exact person, like a name or a birth date.
cards.explanation: Think: does this data point to one exact person?

cards.question: What does “need-to-know” mean?
cards.answer: A person gets only the information that they need for their job.
cards.explanation: It is the idea behind least privilege.

paragraphes: You find your diary. The lock is closed and nothing is missing. But some sentences have changed.
Someone wrote in your pages and locked the diary again. Nobody stole anything. The diary still opens.
But you cannot trust it now. You do not know which sentences are yours. In security, this is called losing integrity.

decouverte.titre: It is like a diary written in ink
decouverte.comme: If someone crosses out a word or adds one in ink, you see it at once. If you keep a photocopy, you can find the right version again.
decouverte.enVrai: Integrity means keeping data correct and complete. Only an authorized person can change it. If someone changes it anyway, we must see it easily. The photocopy is like a backup.

decouverte.question: An administrator (the person who manages the company computers) changes the wrong line in a settings file. There is no hacker. Is integrity hit?
options: No, because without a hacker it is not an attack
Yes, because data was changed by mistake
No, because only viruses break integrity
decouverte.answer: Yes, because data was changed by mistake
decouverte.explanation: Integrity can be lost by mistake, not only by attack. Many people think that only attacks count. This is a common trap.

decouverte.titre: It is like your parents' signature
decouverte.comme: Your parents sign your school planner. The signature shows that it was really them. Later, they cannot say, “I did not see it.”
decouverte.enVrai: A digital signature does this job. It shows who wrote the document: this is authenticity. It also stops people from denying their action: this is nonrepudiation. The image stops here: a digital signature is much harder to fake than a pen signature.

decouverte.texte: You download a game. The site also shows a hash. A hash is a short summary of a file, like a fingerprint. Your computer makes it again after the download. If it is different, the file changed on the way. Do not install it.

cards.question: Official definition: “integrity”
cards.answer: Integrity is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.
cards.explanation: In simple words: keep data correct, valid, and complete. Nothing is changed and nothing is missing.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “integrity”?
options: Integrity is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.
Integrity is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, secrecy, and completeness of data and systems.
Integrity is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data only.
Integrity is the concept of limiting the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.
options_why: Secrecy is about confidentiality. The real word is validity.
The real sentence also covers systems.
Integrity is about maintaining accuracy, not limiting it.
cards.answer: Integrity is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.
cards.explanation: The three qualities are accuracy, validity, and completeness.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “integrity” from memory.
cards.answer: Integrity is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.
cards.explanation: Three parts: maintaining accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.

cards.question: Official definition: what integrity ensures
cards.answer: It ensures that data is not manipulated by anyone other than an authorized party with an authorized purpose, and that any unauthorized manipulation is easily identifiable as such.
cards.explanation: In simple words: only authorized people change the data, and any improper change is easy to see.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”. This is the sentence that follows the definition of integrity.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about what integrity ensures from memory.
cards.answer: It ensures that data is not manipulated by anyone other than an authorized party with an authorized purpose, and that any unauthorized manipulation is easily identifiable as such.
cards.explanation: Two protections: only authorized changes, and any other change is easy to spot.

cards.question: Official definition: “authenticity”
cards.answer: Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is genuine and that all parties are who they say they are.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the data is real, and the people are who they say they are.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”. Authenticity is an idea close to integrity.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “authenticity”?
options: Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is secret and that all parties are who they say they are.
Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is genuine and that all parties are who they say they are.
Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is genuine and that all parties are known by the company.
Accountability refers to ensuring that data is genuine and that all parties are who they say they are.
options_why: Secret data is about confidentiality. Authenticity is about genuine data.
The real sentence says who they say they are.
The term here is authenticity.
cards.answer: Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is genuine and that all parties are who they say they are.
cards.explanation: Look at the two halves: the data is genuine, and the parties are who they say they are.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “authenticity” from memory.
cards.answer: Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is genuine and that all parties are who they say they are.
cards.explanation: Two parts: genuine data, and parties who are who they say they are.

cards.question: Official definition: “nonrepudiation”
cards.answer: Nonrepudiation is a legal principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to deny their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).
cards.explanation: In simple words: nobody can say “it was not me” about what they did, such as creating, changing, or deleting data.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”. To repudiate means to deny.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “nonrepudiation”?
options: Nonrepudiation is a technical rule that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to deny their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).

Nonrepudiation is a legal principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that every party is able to hide their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).

Nonrepudiation is a legal principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to deny their actions (e.g., reading, copying, or printing data).

Nonrepudiation is a legal principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to deny their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).
options_why: The real sentence says it is a legal principle.
The idea is that nobody can deny their actions.
The examples are creating, modifying, or deleting data.
cards.answer: Nonrepudiation is a legal principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to deny their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).
cards.explanation: Look at the key parts: legal principle, deny their actions, and creating, modifying, or deleting.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “nonrepudiation” from memory.
cards.answer: Nonrepudiation is a legal principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to deny their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).
cards.explanation: Three parts: a legal principle, no party can deny, and the three actions in brackets.

cards.question: Official definition: “digital signatures”
cards.answer: Digital signatures are the most common mechanisms used to establish authenticity and nonrepudiation in information systems.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a digital signature shows who wrote something, and the writer cannot deny it later.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “digital signatures” from memory.
cards.answer: Digital signatures are the most common mechanisms used to establish authenticity and nonrepudiation in information systems.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the most common mechanisms, authenticity and nonrepudiation, and information systems.

cards.question: A bank worker types 1000 instead of 100 in a transfer. Nobody meant it. Which security goal is lost?
options: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
None, because there was no attack
options_why: Nobody read the amount without the right. The amount was changed.
The transfer went through. Its amount is not correct.
Integrity can be lost by a plain mistake, with no attacker.
cards.answer: Integrity
cards.explanation: A correct number became incorrect. Mistakes can break integrity too.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”: integrity can be hit by malicious acts, human error, or negligence.

cards.question: What is the main goal of integrity?
options: Keep data hidden from outsiders
Keep systems running all day
Keep a log of who read the data
Keep data correct and complete
options_why: This is the goal of confidentiality.
This is the goal of availability.
A log helps to trace actions, but it is not the main goal of integrity.
cards.answer: Keep data correct and complete
cards.explanation: The main goal is that all data stays intact, correct, and reliable.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”.

cards.question: What does a hash help you to see?
options: Who is allowed to open the file
How fast the file will open
If a file was changed
If the file is secret enough
options_why: Access control decides this, not a hash.
A hash does not measure speed.
A hash does not show how secret a file is.
cards.answer: If a file was changed
cards.explanation: If the hash is different from before, the file changed. This helps to protect integrity.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”: the manual lists cryptographic hashes among the integrity measures.

cards.question: A customer says, “I never placed this order,” but she signed it online. Which idea BEST stops this denial?
options: Nonrepudiation, because she cannot deny her action
Authenticity, because it proves the order is real
Availability, because the order was received
Confidentiality, because the order is private
options_why: Authenticity shows the data is real. Nonrepudiation stops the denial.
Availability is about reaching data, not about denial.
Confidentiality limits who can read the order.
cards.answer: Nonrepudiation, because she cannot deny her action
cards.explanation: Nonrepudiation means that no party can deny their actions. A digital signature gives this.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”.

cards.question: A company wants to bring changed files back to a good version. Which measure helps BEST?
options: Encryption of all the company files
A second server in another city
Regular backups of the data
Longer passwords for every user
options_why: Encryption keeps files secret. It does not restore changed files.
This helps availability more than it restores a good version.
Passwords limit access, but they do not bring back a good version.
cards.answer: Regular backups of the data
cards.explanation: Backups let the company restore tampered data to a known-good state.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a good way to protect integrity?
options: Using version control for software
Letting every user change every file
Checking files with cryptographic hashes
Using strict access control
options_why: Version control lets you go back to a good version.
Hashes show if a file was changed.
Strict access control stops unauthorized changes.
cards.answer: Letting every user change every file
cards.explanation: Many people with the right to change files means many chances of a bad change.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”.

cards.question: An administrator changes the wrong line in a settings file. There is no hacker. What is the BEST description?
options: A loss of integrity caused by a human mistake
Not a security problem, because there was no attack
A loss of confidentiality, because the file was opened
A loss of availability, because the system must be restarted
options_why: Mistakes can break integrity, with no attacker.
Nobody saw data they should not see.
Restarting is not the issue. The data became incorrect.
cards.answer: A loss of integrity caused by a human mistake
cards.explanation: Integrity can be lost by malicious acts, human error, oversight, or negligence.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”.

cards.question: What is the difference between authenticity and nonrepudiation?
options: Authenticity stops denial, nonrepudiation shows who is real
They mean the same, so there is no difference at all
Authenticity is about secrecy, nonrepudiation about speed
Authenticity shows who is real, nonrepudiation stops denial
options_why: The two ideas are swapped. Nonrepudiation is the one about denial.
They are close ideas, but each has its own job.
Neither idea is about secrecy or speed.
cards.answer: Authenticity shows who is real, nonrepudiation stops denial
cards.explanation: Authenticity: the data and the people are real. Nonrepudiation: nobody can deny what they did.

cards.question: Which tool is MOST used to give both authenticity and nonrepudiation?
options: Regular backups of all data
Cryptographic hashes alone
Digital signatures
Role-based access control
options_why: Backups help to restore data. They do not show who signed.
A hash shows a change, but not who made the file.
This limits who can reach data. It does not prove who wrote it.
cards.answer: Digital signatures
cards.explanation: Digital signatures are the most common way to show authenticity and nonrepudiation.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”.

cards.question: A company keeps its sales numbers very secret, but some numbers are incorrect. What is the MAIN risk?
options: Competitors may read the numbers
Staff may make bad decisions with incorrect data
Staff may not be able to open the files
The company may not prove who made a file
options_why: The numbers are kept secret, so this is not the issue.
The problem is the content, not the access.
This is about nonrepudiation. The question is about incorrect data.
cards.answer: Staff may make bad decisions with incorrect data
cards.explanation: Without integrity, staff can make improper decisions or take harmful actions.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”.

cards.question: A user says a price file looks changed. What should the manager do FIRST?
options: Check if the change was authorized
Delete the file at once
Fire the last person who used the file
Wait until a customer complains
options_why: This destroys evidence, and the good data may be lost.
This is extreme, and the cause is not known yet.
This is reactive. Checking first is better.
cards.answer: Check if the change was authorized
cards.explanation: A manager should check the facts before acting.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this follows the usual exam advice to check before acting.

cards.question: Name two measures that help protect integrity.
cards.answer: For example: backups and strict access control. Version control and hashes also help.
cards.explanation: They stop bad changes or bring back a good version.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”: data backups, software version control, strict access control, and cryptographic hashes.

cards.question: Why can integrity be lost without any attack?
cards.answer: People make mistakes. An administrator can type a bad command or change the wrong line.
cards.explanation: Integrity can be lost by error, oversight, or negligence too.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”.

cards.question: What is a hash, in simple words?
cards.answer: A short summary of a file, like a fingerprint. If the file changes, the hash changes.
cards.explanation: Compare the two fingerprints to see a change.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this simple explanation is ours. The manual lists cryptographic hashes as an integrity measure.

cards.question: What does it mean to “repudiate” an action?
cards.answer: To deny it, for example by saying “I did not do it.”
cards.explanation: Nonrepudiation means that nobody can do this.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this is the simple meaning of the word.

paragraphes: Your diary is safe. Nobody read it and nobody wrote in it. But you lost the key of the lock.
Tonight you need it, and you cannot open it. It is well protected, but it is no use to you.
In security, this is called losing availability.

decouverte.titre: It is like a cash machine
decouverte.comme: A cash machine can be very safe. But if it is broken on Saturday night, it helps nobody.
decouverte.enVrai: Availability means that authorized people can reach the data when they need it. A long breakdown can make a company lose customers and money. The image stops here: a machine breaks by itself, but an attack can also cause a breakdown.

decouverte.question: A file is on the shared drive of your company. The drive works and the file is not damaged. You try to open it and you see “access denied”. Is the file available?
options: No, because you cannot open it, it does not exist now
Yes, it is available, but you cannot access it
Yes, and everything is fine
decouverte.answer: Yes, it is available, but you cannot access it
decouverte.explanation: The file exists and the drive works, so it is available. But you do not have the permission, so you cannot access it. These two words are close, but they are not the same.

decouverte.comme: Your teacher puts homework online. If you cannot open the folder, you cannot get to it. If it opens as read-only, you cannot write your answer. If it opens after the deadline, it is too late.
decouverte.enVrai: These are three ideas near availability. Accessibility: you can get to it. Usability: you can do what you need with it. Timeliness: you get it within an acceptable time.

decouverte.texte: A company keeps its files with a cloud provider. A contract writes down what the provider promises. For example, the service works almost all the time and answers fast. This contract is called a service level agreement (SLA).

cards.question: Official definition: “availability”
cards.answer: Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that authorized users can access data when they need it.
cards.explanation: In simple words: authorized people can reach the data when they need it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “availability”?
options: Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that any user can access data when they need it.
Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that authorized users can change data when they need it.
Integrity is the concept focused on ensuring that authorized users can access data when they need it.
Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that authorized users can access data when they need it.
options_why: Availability is for authorized users, not for any user.
Availability is about access. Changing data is about integrity.
