cards.answer: Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that authorized users can access data when they need it.
cards.explanation: Look at the key parts: authorized users, access data, and when they need it.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “availability” from memory.
cards.answer: Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that authorized users can access data when they need it.
cards.explanation: Three parts: authorized users, access to data, and when they need it.

cards.question: Official definition: availability in a company (“In enterprise environments…”)
cards.answer: In enterprise environments, the concept of availability entails providing assurance that legitimate parties have timely and uninterrupted access to the systems and data that they need to do their jobs.
cards.explanation: In simple words: in a company, the right people get the systems and data on time, with no breaks.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about availability in a company from memory.
cards.answer: In enterprise environments, the concept of availability entails providing assurance that legitimate parties have timely and uninterrupted access to the systems and data that they need to do their jobs.
cards.explanation: Three parts: assurance for legitimate parties, timely and uninterrupted access, and the systems and data they need.

cards.question: Official definition: “accessibility”
cards.answer: Accessibility refers to the ability and ease of a user to use a resource or access data when needed.
cards.explanation: In simple words: an authorized person can get in. Nothing blocks the way.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”. The manual gives the example of a file moved to a protected folder.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “accessibility”?
options: Accessibility refers to the speed and cost of a user to use a resource or access data when needed.
Accessibility refers to the ability and ease of a user to change a resource or delete data when needed.
Accessibility refers to the ability and ease of a user to use a resource or access data when needed.
Usability refers to the ability and ease of a user to use a resource or access data when needed.
options_why: Accessibility is about ability and ease, not about speed and cost.
Accessibility is about using or reaching data, not changing it.
The term here is accessibility. Usability is a different idea.
cards.answer: Accessibility refers to the ability and ease of a user to use a resource or access data when needed.
cards.explanation: Look at the key parts: ability and ease, use a resource, and access data when needed.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “accessibility” from memory.
cards.answer: Accessibility refers to the ability and ease of a user to use a resource or access data when needed.
cards.explanation: Three parts: ability and ease, using a resource, and accessing data when needed.

cards.question: Official definition: “usability”
cards.answer: Usability refers to the ability of a user to meet their needs with available data.
cards.explanation: In simple words: you can really do what you need with the data. A read-only file is available, but hard to use.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”. The manual gives the example of a read-only document.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “usability”?
options: Usability refers to the ability of a user to reach any file without permission.
Timeliness refers to the ability of a user to meet their needs with available data.
Usability refers to the speed of a system to meet their needs with available data.
Usability refers to the ability of a user to meet their needs with available data.
options_why: Usability is about meeting needs with available data.
The term here is usability.
Usability is about the ability of a user. It is not about the speed of a system.
cards.answer: Usability refers to the ability of a user to meet their needs with available data.
cards.explanation: Look at the key parts: ability of a user, meet their needs, and available data.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “usability” from memory.
cards.answer: Usability refers to the ability of a user to meet their needs with available data.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the ability of a user, to meet their needs, with available data.

cards.question: Official definition: “timeliness”
cards.answer: Timeliness refers to the time expectation for availability of information and resources and is the measure of the time between when information is expected and when it is available for use.
cards.explanation: In simple words: timeliness is the waiting time between when you expect the information and when you can use it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”. The delay is written in a service level agreement (SLA).

cards.question: Say the official definition of “timeliness” from memory.
cards.answer: Timeliness refers to the time expectation for availability of information and resources and is the measure of the time between when information is expected and when it is available for use.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the time expectation, the measure of time, and expected versus available.

cards.question: The online shop is down all Saturday. Nobody read or changed any data. Which security goal is lost?
options: Confidentiality
Availability
Integrity
None, because the data is still safe
options_why: Nobody saw data they should not see.
No data was changed.
Safe data that nobody can reach is still a loss of availability.
cards.answer: Availability
cards.explanation: Authorized people cannot reach the shop when they need it. This is a loss of availability.

cards.question: A file exists and the drive works, but you have no permission to open it. What can we say?
options: It is available, but not accessible
It is accessible to you, but not available
It is available and accessible
It is neither available nor accessible
options_why: The words are swapped. The file exists, so it is available.
Without the permission, you cannot access it.
The file exists and the drive works, so it is available.
cards.answer: It is available, but not accessible
cards.explanation: The file is intact and the drive is up, so it is available. Without permission, it is not accessible.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: You open a document, but only as read-only. You need to edit it. Which idea is missing?
options: Timeliness
Accessibility
Confidentiality
Usability
options_why: The document came on time. The problem is what you can do with it.
You could open the document, so you could get to it.
Nobody read the document without the right.
cards.answer: Usability
cards.explanation: The file is available, but you cannot meet your need. This is a lack of usability.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: A shop's site works on sale day, but each page takes five minutes to show. Which idea is MOST affected?
options: Accessibility
Timeliness
Usability
Confidentiality
options_why: Customers can enter the site. Nothing blocks them.
Customers can shop, but the problem is the time.
Nobody read data in secret.
cards.answer: Timeliness
cards.explanation: The information comes, but too late compared with what people expect.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a threat to availability?
options: A ransomware attack that locks the files of the company
A long power outage in the room with the main servers
A visitor reads a private screen over a shoulder
A hardware failure in the main server
options_why: Ransomware locks files, so people cannot reach them.
Without power, the systems stop.
A broken server stops the service.
cards.answer: A visitor reads a private screen over a shoulder
cards.explanation: Reading a private screen is a threat to confidentiality, not to availability.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: A company needs its website to keep running even if one server breaks. Which measure is BEST?
options: Add redundancy, such as a second ready server
Encrypt all the files on the company servers every night
Train all the staff to check email addresses before sending
Sign every file of the company with a digital signature
options_why: Encryption helps confidentiality. It does not keep the site running.
Training helps confidentiality by reducing mistakes.
Signatures help authenticity and nonrepudiation.
cards.answer: Add redundancy, such as a second ready server
cards.explanation: Redundancy lets the system keep working when one part breaks.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”: backups, redundant storage, backup power, and web application firewalls.

cards.question: A company moves its files to a cloud provider. Which document BEST sets the acceptable delay of the service?
options: A promise by email from the sales person of the provider
A copy of the provider's code of ethics
A written service level agreement (SLA)
A list of the provider's staff
options_why: An informal promise is not a written agreement.
A code of ethics does not set a service delay.
A staff list says nothing about the service level.
cards.answer: A written service level agreement (SLA)
cards.explanation: Timeliness must be agreed upon and written down in a service level agreement.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: A manager plans for availability. Which list of threats is MOST complete?
options: Only attacks done on purpose by hackers or by insiders
Only natural events such as floods and extreme heat
Only old hardware that is close to the end of its life
Attacks, failures, power cuts, and floods
options_why: Availability also depends on failures and natural events.
Attacks, such as DoS and ransomware, also hurt availability.
Hardware is one threat among many others.
cards.answer: Attacks, failures, power cuts, and floods
cards.explanation: The manual says to consider both human-based and naturally occurring threats.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: Which threat to availability is done on purpose?
options: A hard drive that breaks after years of use
A denial-of-service (DoS) attack
A flood that fills the whole server room
An error in some software that was just updated
options_why: A broken drive is not done on purpose.
A flood is a natural event.
A software error is a mistake, not an attack.
cards.answer: A denial-of-service (DoS) attack
cards.explanation: DoS attacks, ransomware, and deleting data on purpose are malicious threats.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: A file is protected by a password that everybody forgot. Which statement is true?
options: Confidentiality is kept, but availability is lost
Both goals are kept, because the file is safe
Integrity is lost, because nobody can check the file
Confidentiality is lost, because nobody controls the file
options_why: Authorized people cannot reach the file, so availability is lost.
The content did not change.
Nobody can read the file, so secrecy is kept.
cards.answer: Confidentiality is kept, but availability is lost
cards.explanation: A protection that is too strong, with no way in for the right people, breaks availability.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this example is ours.

cards.question: Name two measures that help to keep availability.
cards.answer: For example: data backups and redundant storage. Backup power and web application firewalls (WAFs) also help.
cards.explanation: They keep the service running when something breaks.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”. The cloud can add redundancy.

cards.question: What does SLA stand for, and what is it?
cards.answer: Service level agreement. It is a written contract that sets what the provider promises, such as the acceptable delay.
cards.explanation: Think of the cloud contract.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: Give one threat to availability that is done on purpose, and one that is not.
cards.answer: On purpose: a DoS attack, ransomware, or deleting files. Not on purpose: a hardware failure, a software error, a power outage, or a flood.
cards.explanation: Plan for both kinds of threats.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: What does WAF stand for?
cards.answer: Web application firewall. It is a tool that helps protect a website from disruption.
cards.explanation: It is one of the mechanisms that help availability.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability” lists WAFs. The simple description is ours.

paragraphes: In 1989, the internet is very young. Few people use it, mostly researchers.
A group of experts, the Internet Activities Board (IAB), asks how to behave well in this new place.
It publishes a short text of rules. Its name is RFC 1087, “Ethics and the Internet”. An RFC is a public document that describes a rule or an idea about the internet.

decouverte.titre: It is like the rules of a swimming pool
decouverte.comme: At the pool, nobody tells you everything. But there are simple rules: do not bother other swimmers, do not waste water.
decouverte.enVrai: The 1989 text does the same for the internet. It lists five acts that are not acceptable when done on purpose. Getting in without permission. Stopping others from using the internet. Wasting resources. Destroying the integrity of information. Breaking the privacy of users. The image stops here: the internet has no lifeguard.

decouverte.question: You run a program on purpose that wastes the power of your school network. You steal nothing. Is it against ethics, according to RFC 1087?
options: No, because you stole nothing
Yes, because wasting resources is not acceptable
Only if someone catches you
decouverte.answer: Yes, because wasting resources is not acceptable
decouverte.explanation: The text names wasting resources: people, capacity, and computers. Stealing is not the only fault.

decouverte.texte: The manual says that this text from 1989 already fits the CIA Triad and privacy. Getting in without permission is a risk for confidentiality. Destroying the integrity of information is about integrity. Stopping people from using the internet hits availability.

cards.question: Official definition: RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 1 (access, “seeks to…”)
cards.answer: seeks to gain unauthorized access to the resources of the Internet
cards.explanation: In simple words: getting into the resources of the internet without permission.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”. The opening sentence is: “RFC 1087 characterizes as unethical and unacceptable any activity that purposely”.

cards.question: Say the official words of RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 1, from memory.
cards.answer: seeks to gain unauthorized access to the resources of the Internet
cards.explanation: Three parts: seeks to gain, unauthorized access, and the resources of the Internet.

cards.question: Official definition: RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 2 (use, “disrupts…”)
cards.answer: disrupts the intended use of the Internet
cards.explanation: In simple words: stopping the internet from being used as it should be.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: Say the official words of RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 2, from memory.
cards.answer: disrupts the intended use of the Internet
cards.explanation: Three parts: disrupts, the intended use, and the Internet.

cards.question: Official definition: RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 3 (waste, “wastes…”)
cards.answer: wastes resources (people, capacity, computer) through such actions
cards.explanation: In simple words: wasting people, capacity, or computers.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: Say the official words of RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 3, from memory.
cards.answer: wastes resources (people, capacity, computer) through such actions
cards.explanation: The three resources in brackets: people, capacity, computer.

cards.question: Official definition: RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 4 (integrity, “destroys…”)
cards.answer: destroys the integrity of computer-based information
cards.explanation: In simple words: damaging the correct state of information on computers.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: Say the official words of RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 4, from memory.
cards.answer: destroys the integrity of computer-based information
cards.explanation: Three parts: destroys, the integrity, and computer-based information.

cards.question: Official definition: RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 5 (privacy, “compromises…”)
cards.answer: compromises the privacy of users
cards.explanation: In simple words: breaking the privacy of users.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: Say the official words of RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 5, from memory.
cards.answer: compromises the privacy of users
cards.explanation: Three parts: compromises, the privacy, and of users.

cards.question: A student takes down the school network on purpose, so nobody can connect. Which act of RFC 1087 is this?
options: It compromises the privacy of users
It disrupts the intended use of the Internet
It destroys the integrity of computer-based information
It seeks to gain unauthorized access
options_why: Nobody looked at personal data. The service was only blocked.
No information was destroyed or changed.
The student did not try to get in somewhere without permission.
cards.answer: It disrupts the intended use of the Internet
cards.explanation: A service that others want to use is blocked on purpose. This is a disruption of use.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: Who published RFC 1087, “Ethics and the Internet”?
options: The Internet Activities Board (IAB)
(ISC)2, the group that gives the CISSP
The company that built the first web browser
A court of law in the year 1989
options_why: (ISC)2 wrote the CISSP code of ethics, not this memo.
The memo came from a group of experts on the internet, not from a company.
The memo is a statement of policy, not a court decision.
cards.answer: The Internet Activities Board (IAB)
cards.explanation: The IAB released the memo in January 1989.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: Why does RFC 1087 still matter today?
options: It is a law that every country has to follow today
It lists all the tools that a CISSP must use
It was written to help people pass the exam
Its ideas still fit the CIA Triad and privacy
options_why: It is a statement of policy, not a law.
It talks about behavior, not tools.
It is an old memo about the ethical use of the internet.
cards.answer: Its ideas still fit the CIA Triad and privacy
cards.explanation: The memo is old, but its principles are still relevant for a CISSP.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: A student guesses a classmate's password to open his account. Which act of RFC 1087 does this show BEST?
options: Wasting resources such as people or computers
Disrupting the intended use of the Internet
Seeking unauthorized access to resources
Destroying the integrity of information
options_why: The student did not waste anything.
No service was blocked.
Nothing was changed or destroyed.
cards.answer: Seeking unauthorized access to resources
cards.explanation: The student tries to get in without the right. This is unauthorized access.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: A person shares the private messages of users with strangers. Which act of RFC 1087 does this show BEST?
options: Seeking unauthorized access to resources
Compromising the privacy of users
Wasting resources such as people or computers
Disrupting the intended use of the Internet
options_why: The person may already have access. The problem is the sharing.
Nothing was wasted.
No service was blocked.
cards.answer: Compromising the privacy of users
cards.explanation: Private messages were shown to people who should not see them. This breaks the privacy of users.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT one of the unacceptable activities in RFC 1087?
options: Looking up public news on the internet
Wasting resources such as people and computers
Compromising the privacy of users
Destroying the integrity of computer-based information
options_why: This is one of the five activities.
This is one of the five activities.
This is one of the five activities.
cards.answer: Looking up public news on the internet
cards.explanation: Reading public news is normal use of the internet. It is not on the list.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: Which word in RFC 1087 shows that the acts are done on purpose?
options: Intended
Unauthorized
Resources
Purposely
options_why: This word appears in “intended use”. It is not about the act.
This word is about permission, not about purpose.
This word is about what is wasted.
cards.answer: Purposely
cards.explanation: The RFC speaks about any activity that purposely does these things.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: Which act of RFC 1087 is MOST linked to confidentiality?
options: Destroying the integrity of computer-based information
Disrupting the intended use of the Internet
Seeking unauthorized access to resources
Wasting resources such as people and computers
options_why: This act is linked to integrity.
This act is linked to availability.
This act hurts resources and capacity, not secrecy.
cards.answer: Seeking unauthorized access to resources
cards.explanation: Getting in without permission lets people see what they should not see.
cards.explanation_more: The manual says the memo fits the CIA Triad. Outside the manual: the exact match for each act is our reading.

cards.question: A student wastes network capacity by mistake. How does RFC 1087 treat this?
options: It calls every mistake an unacceptable act, like on purpose
It talks about acts done on purpose, not mistakes
It says that mistakes are worse than acts done on purpose
It says that only the network owner can decide what to do
options_why: The RFC talks about acts that are done on purpose.
The RFC does not say this.
The RFC does not name an owner for this.
cards.answer: It talks about acts done on purpose, not mistakes
cards.explanation: The key word is “purposely”. A mistake is still a security issue, but it is not what the RFC describes.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: this is our reading of the word “purposely”.

cards.question: Which resources does the RFC list when it talks about waste?
options: Money, time, and electricity for the building
Passwords, keys, badges, and access cards
People, capacity, and computers
Servers, routers, cables, and other network parts
options_why: These are costs, but the RFC lists other resources.
These are access items, not the listed resources.
These are parts of a network, but the RFC lists other resources.
cards.answer: People, capacity, and computers
cards.explanation: The three resources in brackets are people, capacity, and computer.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: When did the Internet Activities Board publish “Ethics and the Internet” (RFC 1087)?
cards.answer: In January 1989.
cards.explanation: This was around the dawn of the internet.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: What is an RFC?
cards.answer: A public document that describes a rule or an idea about the internet.
cards.explanation: RFC 1087 is a statement of policy.
cards.explanation_more: Outside the manual: RFC stands for “Request for Comments”.

cards.question: Why is a text from 1989 still useful for a professional today?
cards.answer: Its principles about access, use, integrity, and privacy still fit the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation: Tools change, but principles stay the same.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: What does IAB stand for?
cards.answer: Internet Activities Board.
cards.explanation: It is the group that published RFC 1087.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

concepts.name: The limits of the triad (NIST, privacy)

paragraphes: You get a message from your best friend: “Send me your password, fast!”
The message came on time, it is not changed, and nobody else read it. But your friend did not write it.
The three pillars do not see this problem. This is one limit of the triad. Experts tried to fix it.

decouverte.question: A secret message comes on time and is not changed. But it comes from a fake friend. Which idea is missing from the CIA Triad?
options: Availability
Authenticity: knowing who really wrote it
Confidentiality
decouverte.answer: Authenticity: knowing who really wrote it
decouverte.explanation: The manual says the triad does not directly deal with authenticity or nonrepudiation. The other two pillars were respected here.

decouverte.titre: It is like a game with three rules
decouverte.comme: A game has three simple rules. With more players, new cases appear that the rules do not cover. So people add new rules.
decouverte.enVrai: The triad is simple, and this is its strength. It comes from work in the mid-1960s. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) added two ideas in a paper called SP 800-33.

decouverte.titre: It is like a sign-in sheet
decouverte.comme: At school, a sign-in sheet shows who came in and when. If a page goes missing, you can find out who took it.
decouverte.enVrai: This is accountability: each action can be traced to one person or system. Without it, nobody knows who did what.

decouverte.titre: It is like testing the fire alarm
decouverte.comme: A fire alarm is tested every month. Not to set it off, but to be sure it will work on the day there is smoke.
decouverte.enVrai: This is assurance: confidence that the protections really work as planned. A company must not only install protections. It must be able to trust them.

decouverte.texte: You keep private photos on your phone. Only you decide who sees them and who shares them. This is the idea of privacy. For a company, it means the data of customers and workers. Privacy is close to confidentiality, but it covers only data about people.

cards.question: Official definition: “accountability”
cards.answer: accountability (that actions of an entity may be traced uniquely to that entity)
cards.explanation: In simple words: each action can be traced back to one person or system only.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”. NIST SP 800-33 adds accountability and assurance to the triad.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “accountability”?
options: accountability (that actions of an entity may be traced uniquely to that entity)
accountability (that actions of an entity may be hidden from that entity)
accountability (that passwords of an entity may be traced uniquely to that entity)
assurance (that actions of an entity may be traced uniquely to that entity)
options_why: The real idea is that actions are traced uniquely to the entity.
Accountability is about actions, not passwords.
The term here is accountability. Assurance is a different idea.
cards.answer: accountability (that actions of an entity may be traced uniquely to that entity)
cards.explanation: Look at the key parts: actions of an entity, traced uniquely, and to that entity.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “accountability” from memory.
cards.answer: accountability (that actions of an entity may be traced uniquely to that entity)
cards.explanation: Three parts: the actions of an entity, traced uniquely, to that same entity.

cards.question: Official definition: “assurance”
cards.answer: assurance (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both technical and operational, work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
cards.explanation: In simple words: you have good reasons to trust that the protections really work.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”. Technical means the tools. Operational means the way they are used.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “assurance”?
options: assurance (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both legal and financial, work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
assurance (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both technical and operational, are installed to protect only the system)
accountability (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both technical and operational, work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
assurance (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both technical and operational, work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
options_why: The real sentence says technical and operational.
The real sentence also covers the information, and the measures must work as intended.
The term here is assurance.
cards.answer: assurance (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both technical and operational, work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
cards.explanation: Look at the key parts: basis for confidence, technical and operational, and work as intended.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “assurance” from memory.
cards.answer: assurance (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both technical and operational, work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
cards.explanation: Three parts: the basis for confidence, technical and operational measures, and work as intended.

cards.question: Official definition: “privacy”
cards.answer: Privacy, as defined in the (ISC)2 glossary, is the right of human individuals to control the distribution of information about themselves.
cards.explanation: In simple words: people decide who gets the information about them.

cards.question: We can find out which employee deleted a file. Which idea is this?

paragraphes: Your friend loses a USB stick on the bus. His homework is on it. The files are encrypted. This means they are locked with a secret code, so nobody can read them.
The homework is not changed. But someone else now holds the stick in a pocket. Your friend has lost control of where his information is.
A pioneer of security, Donn B. Parker, added new ideas to the triad for cases like this.

decouverte.titre: It is like a die with six faces
decouverte.comme: A die has six clear faces. No face copies another, and each face has its own number.
decouverte.enVrai: Parker's hexad has six ideas: the three pillars of the triad, and three new ones. Parker wanted each idea to be atomic (it cannot be split further) and nonoverlapping (each one is different from the others).

decouverte.question: You lose an encrypted USB stick on the bus. Which of Parker's ideas is hit the most?
options: Possession or control
Utility
Authenticity
decouverte.explanation: The data is not read or changed, but you do not know where the stick is. The other two ideas are tempting, but they are about something else.

decouverte.titre: It is like a recipe in a language you do not know
decouverte.comme: You have a cake recipe, complete and correct. But it is written in a language that you do not know. You have it, but it is no use to you.
decouverte.enVrai: This is utility: is the information useful to the person who has it? Information can be available and still not useful.

decouverte.texte: An email comes in your director's name. Authenticity asks: who really wrote it? A file is encrypted and its key is lost: utility is lost. A USB stick is stolen: possession or control is lost.

cards.question: Official definition: Parkerian Hexad, “Confidentiality”
cards.answer: Confidentiality: The limits on who has access to information
cards.explanation: In simple words: who is allowed to get to the information.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.answer: Integrity: Whether the information is in its intended state

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.question: Say the official line for “Integrity” in the Parkerian Hexad from memory.
cards.answer: Integrity: Whether the information is in its intended state
cards.explanation: Three parts: whether, the information, and its intended state.

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.question: Say the official line for “Availability” in the Parkerian Hexad from memory.
cards.answer: Availability: Whether the information can be accessed in a timely manner

cards.question: Say the official line for “Authenticity” in the Parkerian Hexad from memory.
cards.answer: Authenticity: The proper attribution of the person who created the information

cards.answer: Utility: The usefulness of the information

cards.question: Say the official line for “Utility” in the Parkerian Hexad from memory.

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.question: Say the official line for “Possession or control” in the Parkerian Hexad from memory.
cards.answer: Possession or control: The physical state where the information is maintained

cards.question: Parker keeps the CIA Triad and adds three ideas. Which ones?
options: Authenticity, utility, possession or control
Accountability, assurance, and the privacy of data
Authenticity, nonrepudiation, and privacy of people
Encryption, backup, and firewall
options_why: These come from NIST and from the manual, not from Parker's hexad.
Only authenticity is in the hexad.
These are protection measures, not ideas of the model.
cards.answer: Authenticity, utility, possession or control
cards.explanation: These three additions, with the triad, make six ideas. This is the hexad.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.question: An encrypted USB stick is lost on a bus. The data is not read or changed. Which hexad idea is hit the MOST?
options: Utility, because the data may be hard to use
Authenticity, because someone may pretend to be the owner
Integrity, because the stick may be damaged
Possession or control, because the stick is gone
options_why: Utility is about how useful the information is. The issue here is where the stick is.
Nobody pretended to be someone else.
The data was not changed.
cards.answer: Possession or control, because the stick is gone
cards.explanation: The data may stay secret, but the owner no longer controls where the information is.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.question: What does “atomic” mean for Parker's ideas?
options: It can be shared between two teams in a company
It is true for every company in every country
It cannot be broken down into smaller ideas
It is the first idea in the list
options_why: Atomic means that an idea cannot be split further.
Atomic is about splitting an idea, not about companies.
Atomic is not about order.
cards.answer: It cannot be broken down into smaller ideas
cards.explanation: An atomic idea cannot be broken down further.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.question: A file arrives on time, but you cannot read its language. Which hexad idea does this BEST show is missing?

The file is with you.

Availability
Possession or control
Authenticity

The email arrived, so it is available.

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT one of the six ideas of Parker's hexad?

This is the third idea of the hexad.

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.question: A company loses an encrypted laptop in a taxi. Which statement BEST describes the loss?

Control of the device is lost, even if the data stays secret

The data is no longer important to the company

Nothing suggests that data was changed.
The data is still important. The company lost the device.
cards.answer: Control of the device is lost, even if the data stays secret
cards.explanation: The secret can stay protected while physical control is lost.

cards.question: Which hexad idea talks about data being accessed in a “timely manner”?
options: Integrity
Utility
Possession or control
Availability

Utility talks about usefulness.

cards.answer: Availability

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.question: Which idea did Parker add, so it is not in the CIA Triad?
options: Utility
Integrity
Availability
Confidentiality

It is already in the triad.
It is already in the triad.

cards.question: Why did Parker want ideas that are “nonoverlapping”?

So that the model has fewer than six ideas
So that no idea repeats another idea
So that every idea uses its own tools

The model has six ideas.
Ideas are not tied to tools.

cards.explanation: Parker wanted ideas that are both atomic and nonoverlapping.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

cards.question: Who proposed the most widely accepted extension of the CIA Triad?
